## Key R functions used in this notebook

This page collects every new R function you used in this tutorial, in one place, as a quick-reference glossary. Each function below follows the same format:

- **Package:** where the function comes from. Most functions in this tutorial come from **ggplot2**, the plotting package loaded automatically when you run `library(tidyverse)`. A few come from other packages, or from **Base R** (built into R, no setup needed).
- **What it does:** a plain-English explanation, no jargon.
- **Why you'd use it:** the everyday analyst reason you'd reach for it.
- **Arguments:** the inputs you put inside the parentheses `()` to tell the function exactly what to work on. Some are required, some are optional. Arguments listed here are not necessarily exhaustive.
- **Example:** the function used on this week's `housing` dataset.

For more information on any function, use ?`function_name` in the R console (e.g. `?ggplot`) to see the official documentation, which includes a full list of arguments, descriptions, and often many examples.

### `ggplot()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Starts a new plot and tells R which dataset to build it from.

**Why you'd use it:** It's the very first step of building any chart with ggplot2. Every plot in this tutorial starts with a call to `ggplot()`.

**Arguments:**

- `data` — the data frame you want to plot, for example `housing`.
- `mapping` — usually an `aes()` call that tells ggplot2 which columns to use for which part of the plot (see `aes()` below).

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Start a plot using the housing data, with region on the x-axis
ggplot(housing, aes(x = regionname))
```

### `aes()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Maps columns in your data to visual features of the plot, such as which column goes on the x-axis, which goes on the y-axis, or which column controls the fill color of bars.

**Why you'd use it:** It's how you tell ggplot2 "this column goes here on the chart." Almost every plot you build needs an `aes()` mapping.

**Arguments (in plain English):**

- `x` — the column shown along the horizontal axis.
- `y` — the column shown along the vertical axis. Not always needed, since some charts (like bar charts and histograms) can count rows automatically.
- `fill` — the column used to color the inside of bars or bins, handy for comparing groups within the same chart.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Map price to the x-axis and dwelling type to the fill color
aes(x = price, fill = type)
```

### `geom_bar()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Draws bars. By default, it counts how many rows of data fall into each category and draws a bar for each one.

**Why you'd use it:** To see how many observations you have in each category, for example how many listings are in each region.

**Arguments:**

- an optional `aes()` — lets you override the default counting, for example to plot a proportion instead of a raw count.
- `fill` — a fixed color for all the bars, when you're not mapping fill to a column.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = regionname)) +
  geom_bar()
```

### `labs()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Adds or changes the text labels on a plot, such as the axis titles and the main title.

**Why you'd use it:** Raw column names like `regionname` don't mean much to an audience. `labs()` lets you replace them with clear, readable text.

**Arguments:**

- `x` — text for the x-axis label.
- `y` — text for the y-axis label.
- `title` — text for the plot title.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
labs(
  x = "Region",
  y = "Count",
  title = "Number of Listings by Region"
)
```

### `geom_histogram()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Draws a histogram. It splits a numeric variable into evenly sized bins and draws a bar showing how many rows fall into each bin.

**Why you'd use it:** To see the distribution of a continuous variable, such as how house prices are spread out across the market.

**Arguments:**

- `bins` — how many bins to split the data into. More bins show finer detail, fewer bins give a smoother picture.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50)
```

### `facet_wrap()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Splits one plot into a grid of smaller plots, one panel per category.

**Why you'd use it:** To compare patterns across groups side by side, for example comparing the price distribution of each dwelling type in its own panel.

**Arguments:**

- a formula starting with `~`, naming the column to split the plot by, for example `~ type`.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  facet_wrap(~ type)
```

### `geom_point()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Draws a scatter plot, one dot for every row of data.

**Why you'd use it:** To see the relationship between two numeric variables, for example how price relates to distance from the city center.

**Arguments:**

- `alpha` — how see-through each point is, from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid). Lower values help when many points overlap.
- `color` — the color of the points.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = distance, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05)
```

### `geom_smooth()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Adds a fitted trend line through your data.

**Why you'd use it:** To summarize the overall relationship between two variables, cutting through the noise of individual data points.

**Arguments:**

- `method` — the type of line to fit, for example `"lm"` for a straight regression line.
- `se` — whether to show a shaded confidence band around the line. Set to `FALSE` to hide it.
- `linewidth` — how thick the line is.
- `color` — the color of the line.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = distance, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1)
```

### `scale_x_continuous()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Controls how the x-axis of a plot is drawn: for example, whether it uses a log scale, and how the numbers on it are formatted.

**Why you'd use it:** Price data is often skewed, with a few very expensive listings stretching the axis. A log scale spreads out the clustered, lower values so patterns are easier to see. You can also use it to format axis numbers as currency.

**Arguments:**

- `trans` — a transformation to apply to the axis, for example `"log10"`.
- `labels` — how to format the axis numbers, for example `scales::dollar` to show them as currency.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = price, fill = type)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10", labels = scales::dollar)
```

### `scale_fill_okabe_ito()`

**Package:** ggokabeito

**What it does:** Applies a colorblind-friendly set of colors to whatever is mapped to `fill` in your plot.

**Why you'd use it:** So your charts can be read clearly by everyone, including people with color vision deficiencies. This is the default color palette for this course.

**Arguments:** none used in this tutorial. It's called with empty parentheses.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = price, fill = type)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito()
```

### `theme_bw()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Switches the plot to a clean black-and-white theme, with a white background and light gray gridlines, instead of ggplot2's default gray background.

**Why you'd use it:** It's often easier to read and looks more polished for a business report or presentation.

**Arguments:** none used in this tutorial. It's called with empty parentheses.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(housing, aes(x = regionname)) +
  geom_bar() +
  theme_bw()
```

### `theme()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Fine-tunes specific visual details of a plot, such as rotating axis text, centering the title, or hiding the legend.

**Why you'd use it:** For polishing the presentation of a plot once the data and layers are already in place.

**Arguments used in this tutorial:**

- `axis.text.x` — the x-axis tick labels, set using `element_text()`, for example to rotate crowded labels.
- `plot.title` — the plot title text, set using `element_text()`, for example to center it.
- `legend.position` — where the legend appears. Set to `"none"` to remove it entirely.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
... +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 55, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

### `element_text()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Describes how a specific piece of plot text should look, such as its angle or alignment. It's used inside `theme()`, not on its own.

**Why you'd use it:** To rotate crowded axis labels so they don't overlap, or to center a title.

**Arguments:**

- `angle` — how many degrees to rotate the text.
- `hjust` — the horizontal alignment of the text, a value between 0 and 1.
- `vjust` — the vertical alignment of the text, a value between 0 and 1.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))
```

### `scale_y_continuous()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Controls how the y-axis numbers of a plot are formatted.

**Why you'd use it:** To display the y-axis as dollars, as a percentage, or in some other readable format instead of plain numbers.

**Arguments:**

- `labels` — how to format the axis numbers, for example `scales::dollar` or `scales::percent`.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```

### `ggsave()`

**Package:** ggplot2

**What it does:** Saves a plot to a file on your computer, such as a PDF or PNG image.

**Why you'd use it:** To export a finished chart so you can include it in a report, slide deck, or send it to someone else.

**Arguments:**

- `filename` — the file name (and file type) to save to, in quotation marks, for example `"combined_price_plots.pdf"`.
- `plot` — *(optional)* which plot object to save. If you leave this out, `ggsave()` saves the most recently displayed plot.
- `width`, `height` — the size of the saved image.

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggsave("combined_price_plots.pdf", plot = combined_plot, width = 12, height = 8)
```
